transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today? Is there something specific that’s been troubling you?

Well, doctor, thank you for seeing me. I... I came in because I just, well, I can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It's just awful and it's been weighing on me so heavily. Take my kitchen table, for instance. We can't even eat on it right now. It is completely covered—just piles and piles everywhere—with my husband’s appointment papers. He’s been having to see the doctors quite a bit lately, you know how it is at our age, and there's all this paperwork and after-visit summaries they send home. 

And mixed in with all of his things are all these church flyers, because I try to stay involved with the Sunday committee, and then there are the senior-center notes... and lists. Oh, the lists. I have all these half-finished to-do lists written on the backs of envelopes and scrap paper scattered everywhere. A grocery list with only three things on it, a list of phone calls I need to make but never do. 

And the terrible part is, I’ll pull out a chair and sit there at the table, just staring at the mess, and I sit there not knowing which thing to do first. Should I sort the medical bills? Should I read the church bulletin? Should I finish the grocery list? I just freeze. My mind goes completely blank, and I sit there for so long trying to figure out where to even begin until the whole day is just gone. The sun starts going down, my husband comes in asking about dinner, and the entire day is just gone. Poof. And the table looks exactly the same as it did at breakfast. I just don't understand why I can't just organize a simple pile of papers...

Can you tell me if this difficulty starting tasks or feeling stuck like at the table happens in other parts of your life, too—like in getting dressed, doing laundry, or even just getting out of bed in the morning?

Well, no, not... not exactly like that. I mean, getting out of bed is fine, usually. I wake up, and I know I have to get up, so I do. And getting dressed, well, I just put on whatever is comfortable these days. I don't really have anywhere fancy to go, so a nice pair of slacks and a sweater is usually just fine. I don't stand in the closet agonizing over it or anything like that. 

And the laundry... well, the laundry gets done eventually. I might leave it in the basket a bit longer than I should, or maybe it sits in the dryer until it's terribly wrinkled and I have to run it again with a damp towel to steam the wrinkles out—which, you know, my mother would just be appalled by. She used to iron everything, even the sheets! Can you imagine ironing sheets these days? But no, I wouldn't say I freeze up looking at the washing machine the way I do with the papers on the table. 

It’s really just... it’s the organizing. The sorting. The things that require me to make a decision about what goes where, or what needs to be handled right this very second versus what can wait until Tuesday. That’s where I just hit a brick wall. The daily routine things, the physical things like making a cup of tea or putting on my shoes, those just happen. But if you ask me to sit down and figure out a plan for the day, or go through the mail, or even just decide which bill to pay first when there are three of them sitting there... that's when my brain just stops working. It's like a car engine that just stalls out completely. So, no, I wouldn't say I get stuck getting dressed or anything like that. It's just the... the mental clutter, I suppose you could call it.
Have you been feeling down, sad, or losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, even things like church or the senior center?

Well, no, not sad. I wouldn't use the word sad. I mean, I love my church group, I really do. The ladies there are just wonderful, especially Martha, she always brings these lovely little lemon bars that her grandmother used to make, though I think she uses a bit too much powdered sugar on top, but that's neither here nor there. I still enjoy going. I still want to go. It's just... I can't seem to get myself organized enough to actually participate the way I used to. 

It’s not that I’ve lost interest, doctor, not at all! I still care very deeply about the Sunday committee and the senior center. I just... I feel so overwhelmed by the mess and the disorganization that I end up missing things. Like last week, I fully intended to go to the senior center for the Tuesday morning social—they were having a guest speaker talk about container gardening, and you know, I used to have a beautiful garden when we lived in our old house, tomatoes as big as softballs! But I couldn't find the flyer with the time on it, because it was buried under my husband's cardiology reports, and by the time I finally unearthed it, the social was already half over. 

So it's not a feeling of being down or depressed, or not wanting to do things. I want to do them! I just feel terribly frustrated with myself. I feel guilty, really, because I know I should be able to manage these simple things. I mean, I'm a grown woman, I've run a household for forty years, and now I can't even keep track of a Tuesday morning social. It just makes me feel foolish and scattered, but no, I wouldn't say I'm sitting around crying or feeling blue or anything like that. Just... very, very frustrated that my brain won't cooperate with what I actually want to be doing.
When you sit at the table looking at the mess and feel stuck, do you feel anxious or overwhelmed in that moment, like your mind is racing or your body feels tense?

Well, anxious... I suppose that depends on what you mean by anxious. I don't feel like I'm having a panic attack, you know, like they show on television where people are breathing into a paper bag. My heart isn't pounding out of my chest, and I don't feel like I'm going to faint or anything dramatic like that. My hands don't shake. I remember when my sister, Helen, used to get anxious before flying—she would literally tremble, her whole body would just shake, and she’d have to take a little pill just to get on the airplane. It’s nothing like that. 

But overwhelmed? Oh, yes. Terribly overwhelmed. It's more of a... a heaviness. Like a physical weight pressing down on my shoulders. I sit there and look at that pile of papers—the electric bill sticking out from under the church bulletin, the little sticky notes I wrote to myself about calling the plumber that are now stuck to my husband's blood test results—and my mind doesn't race, exactly. It’s almost the opposite. It’s like it gets stuck in the mud. 

I don't feel tense in my muscles, not like I'm clenching my jaw or balling my fists. It’s just this profound sense of being completely paralyzed by the sheer volume of it all. I look at it, and I think, "Okay, I need to pay the electric bill." But then I think, "Wait, I need the checkbook." And then I remember the checkbook is in my purse, which is in the hallway. But to get to the hallway, I have to walk past the laundry basket, and I remember I never started the dryer. And before I've even stood up from the chair, I'm exhausted. Just completely, utterly exhausted by the thought of trying to untangle it all. So I just sit there. I don't feel panicked, I just feel... defeated, I suppose. Like the pile has won, and I'm just sitting there staring at it while the clock ticks away the whole afternoon.
Doctor: Have you been feeling more tired than usual or lacking energy, even when you haven't done anything physically or mentally exhausting?

Well, tired... no, I wouldn't say I feel tired in that way. If I haven't been trying to tackle that mess on the table, my energy is actually quite good for a woman my age! I mean, I sleep just fine, usually. My husband, now, he’s always dozing off in his recliner with the golf channel blaring—honestly, I don't know how anyone can sleep through that announcer's voice, but he manages it every single afternoon like clockwork. But me? No, I'm up and about. I still walk down to the end of the driveway to get the mail every day, and I can stand at the stove and make a full pot roast with carrots and potatoes without needing to sit down and rest, which is certainly more than I can say for some of the ladies in my neighborhood. Susan, for instance, she had her knee replaced last fall, bless her heart, and she still complains she can't stand for more than ten minutes at a time. 

But my body feels perfectly fine. I have plenty of energy to do things around the house. If I'm just puttering around, you know, watering my African violets—I have three of them on the windowsill above the kitchen sink, and they are just blooming beautifully right now, such a vibrant, deep purple, I really must remember to give them a little fertilizer next week—if I'm just doing pleasant little things like that, I feel absolutely fine. I don't wake up feeling drained or sluggish or anything like that. 

It's really just like I was saying before, that deep, heavy exhaustion only ever hits me when I have to sit down and try to organize things. That’s what drains me. But if you're asking if I just feel tired out of the blue, for no reason at all, when I haven't done anything? No, not at all. As long as I don't have to figure out a schedule or sort through paperwork, I have all the energy in the world.
